Title: why french people don't do deals ??

Messages.Author: Reyda
Messages.Body:
Maybe, after reading the reports of the Wonderful Watford tournament you'll
find strange that a guy going to the finals doesn't make deals at all !

In france, you'll almost never see deals , not in friendly games, nor in
tournaments. Is there a particular reason ? I think that, first, we try to
play our deck the best way. Even if our prey, or predator , or both, has
"the screw me if i sit next" deck. I remember, myself, in Watford, playing a
political deck with max +2 stealth, didn't made a deal with my Tzimisce
prey. I tried, and i waited until my prey took too much confidence and run
low on pool. I let him intercept my previous votes, playing no stealth to
keep him confident. When he used a "Thelepatic counter" to intercept one of
my votes, i knew it was the time to strike =) that's part of our metagame !
every good players does that here. There is a french word "contre mauvaise
fortune bon coeur", wich means approx. "be light hearted against bad odds".
Sometime we prefer trying and diying rather than gaining one or two VP from
another player's hands.
The second reason is, we there think making complete deals involving VP
split (I gain 3 then i roll over and you gain 2) is an "inferior" version of
King making, with one or two VP as a "tip" for loyal service. And above all
King Making sounds bad for us : y'all remember we guillotin'ed our royal
court, don't you =)

so, to resume : it's a mix of mentality and pride, i think, which make us
think that making VP split is simply not a french affair =)

comments welcome ;)
reyda

"Reyda" <re...@noos.fr> wrote in message news:<9k4crc$nj1$1...@hadron.noos.net>...

I gained 4 vps in the final to win and didn't make a single deal.
Admittedly my deck was somewhat single minded in the way it focussed
on it's prey, but I am firmly of the opinion that you do not have to
deal to win an English tourney. It may help, and some of the best
players may well be defined by their abilities to deal (no hard
feelings Rob:-), but games are generally played at the level of the
decks on the table not of the people playing those decks. before
everyone jumps on this comment, let me explain what I mean: Someone
playing a weenie dominate bleed deck is going to have real problems
dealing, but still can win. Whereas someone playing a deck containing
votes should at least to open to deals to supliment the cards at their
disposal. A bleed deck has to focus forward and defend backward, a
rush deck, to some extent, has to balance both concerns and be open to
the possibility that it may not have the bleed potential to sweep, and
therefore a deal could be the best option in getting vps. A vote deck,
realistically, can never guarentee a vote lock, so dealing becomes the
main strategy. It's another way to maximise, not only vps, but deck
performance as well. But it is not the only way and it is certainly
not the best way.

Tony

Messages.Author: James Coupe
Messages.Body:
In message <19048d48.01073...@posting.google.com>, Tony
<ztr...@yahoo.com> writes

[table dealing]

>It may help, and some of the best
>players may well be defined by their abilities to deal (no hard
>feelings Rob:-), but games are generally played at the level of the
>decks on the table not of the people playing those decks.

I'd disagree here, to a certain extent.

All games, of course, to some extent rely on:

- seating position
- deck composition
- starting position (number of transfers etc.)
- luck
- deck composition
- deck composition with respect to metagame
- uncontrolled draw

and so on, I'd argue that social play/diplomacy/agitation/whatever you
want to call it can be a potent weapon in the right hands.

Some decks are, by definition, slow. e.g. Matt Green's deck[0] at
Watford would take a few turns to get going, whereas yours would be able
to get going much more quickly. Since he had a lot riding on two 8
point vampires, he couldn't ever really motor until both came out. (Not
entirely true, since he could do some stuff with just one of course, but
the deck needs two vampires out to function.) Agitation is a perfectly
valid speed defence, if you can pull it off. It works especially well
in non-bleed decks, simply because you have the ability to tempt the
Methuselah.

"Well, Mr Grand Predator, if you tap out now, I'll be able to call this
Kine Resources Contested (*waves green back of card in hand enticingly*)
with 2 points against your predator. Oh, and I'll be able to play this
Bribes on it too. What, you have a vote from Caitlin? Oh my."

In the same way, of course, that not all elements of defence/attack are
necessary to function and function well (indeed, all elements may be
counter-productive), agitation is one that many decks may throw to the
wind. But it's not without its merit.

And agitation can *only* rely on the skill of the player. Agitation
needs a deck that can work on it, sure, but a player who's good at
agitation can play Skin of Steel for combat defence just as easily as
the poor agitation player.

I'd also disagree with the idea that the deck is more important than the
player. The player plays the deck, the player drives the game. If it
was *only* the deck, many of those copying the tournament winning decks
and playing them would surely do better than they.

[0] *drool* *spurt* That deck is lush. I want one.

--

Messages.Author: Matt Latham
Messages.Body:
I truly dislike the Succubus Club style of dealing. Whats the point of
playing a game when two people can coordinate to split all the points? If
offered such a deal I'd decline.

I come to tournaments to play the friggin game. Yes, politics are a part of
the game, but the whole "I keep everyone off your back and give you whatever
resourses you need via the Club to kill three people, then you roll for me"
is not politics, its borderline collusion.

My opinions are my own, but I must agree with the stance of my esteemed
French collegues.

Matt

What I saw at Origins which I heard later is not "uncommon".

Player A has Sucubus club. Player B is Player A's prey. Player A tells
player B to go full bore at his prey, and that player A will act as a wall
behind B. Player A and B will use the Succubus club to shunt resources back
and forth to maximize dead prey in front and to render Player A's predator
powerless. Once the A-B Combine has killed each prey in turn, Player B uses
the Succubus club to transfer all pool to Player A, giving B 3 VP's and A 2
VP's.

Messages.Author: Rob Treasure
Messages.Body:
"Tony" <ztr...@yahoo.com> wrote in message

> I gained 4 vps in the final to win and didn't make a single deal.
> Admittedly my deck was somewhat single minded in the way it focussed

> deal to win an English tourney. It may help, and some of the best
> players may well be defined by their abilities to deal (no hard
> feelings Rob:-), but games are generally played at the level of the
> decks on the table not of the people playing those decks.

>But it is not the only way and it is certainly

> not the best way.
>
> Tony

Have to disagree with you there on a massive scale Tony (did you expect any
less ?). I am totally of the belief that a consistently successful player
uses all means to win at his / her disposal. This includes (where
appropriate to deck type and situation) the full range of agitation and deal
making skills.

As I have said in many of my newsletters and general commentary, the player
who actively decides 'not to deal' is IMO robbing themselves of one of the
sharpest swords in the game.

I put it to you that you won by taking advantage of a good opportunity,
having little or no pressure on you, playing your focussed deck well and NOT
AT ALL by declining to make deals. As we discussed at length at the tourney,
your deck did not lend itself at all to deal making (I guess
counterproductive cross table Deflections would be about all it could offer)
and as such no player on the table sought to make deals with you. All being
experienced 'identification players' we had seen what your deck did and knew
exactly what you intended to do with it :o) Which is exactly why you felt
'left out' of the deal making on the table.

The sort of deck that you played tends to be seen by others as a huge threat
to the balance of the table. In any other situation I would have had no
qualms what so ever in enlisting the help of any / all other players on the
table to stamp on a Weenie deck. Part of my (and many, many other players)
game centres around balancing the table and talking to achieve such an end.
A deck such as yours is bound to unsettle as it can oust very quickly and
comes out of the blocks bleeding for 6-10 per turn.

In hindsight, had I known that you were packing 10 Deflections (you filthy
man :o) there is no way I would have chosen to bleed you, but then again
Francois would have very possibly sat down somewhere different after me.
Ideally I should have sat behind Francios with you bleeding me, but as I
said - hindsight... bloody table order :o(

I would also add as an aside that had you chosen to make deals, it would IMO
have only served to strengthen your table position and make your job easier.
Even a player playing a weenie dom or pre deck can establish others as the
bad guys on the table and enlist aid in taking them down.

Again, extremely well done for winning man, but don't lose sight of the
final that we played.

Rob

[off-topically...]

Ithaca? Are they still playing serious VTES there? I mean, I'm
sure Peter is. But I thought the hardcore competition kinda
dwindled away after James Hamblin and I graduated and moved away.
(Not to imply that I think we were the Best Players Ever, but I
think we were the last ones still around, besides Peter, who were
very interested in competitive Jyhad.)

And then, even when we were there, we didn't exactly have a big
tournament scene - we played a lot of fierce games every week (or
more often) but we didn't have tournaments more than a couple times
a year. Honestly I don't think it really compared to LA or the
London-area scene or anything like that. Although we did certainly
have a hotly-evolving metagame and some innovation.

Ah, the good old days of blowing off class and playing Jyhad all
day in the dorm basement...

> How good can we be? I mean, I routinely make the finals in local
> tournaments.

Hard to argue with that. ;-)

On-topically, I've found dealmaking very prevalent everywhere
I've played, which is almost everywhere on the east coast of the
US. And my playgroup dealmakes a lot in our regular (non-tourney)
games as well. But we don't usually use the Succubus Club to do
it... at least not yet. (I have seen one a couple times recently,
but I haven't seen it have any huge effects yet.)

As a dealmaker myself, I don't see anything wrong with making deals,
particularly in situations where you'd otherwise be totally screwed
by the decks you're next to. Everyone's trying to win the game,
right? And if you're sitting next to your deck's nemesis, you're
a lot more likely to do well if you make some kind of deal, yeah?

If you take the "try and (probably) die" approach, aren't you
just kingmaking in favor of your predator (and, to some extent,
your prey) rather than somebody else? Why is this more acceptable
than explicitly helping someone in return for a better chance at
getting some VPs of your own?

Sure, playing your deck to do what it was designed to do is nice,
and it's part of the game. But in any multiplayer game, playing
the other players is at least as important as playing the deck. I
know VTES was designed to reduce the importance of diplomacy, but
it's still important - just not as crucial as it could have been.

Josh

"Rob Treasure" <Rob.Tr...@btinternet.com> wrote in message news:<9k6rlj$2u8pb$1...@ID-99315.news.dfncis.de>...

> "Tony" <ztr...@yahoo.com> wrote in message
>
> > I gained 4 vps in the final to win and didn't make a single deal.
> > Admittedly my deck was somewhat single minded in the way it focussed
> > on it's prey, but I am firmly of the opinion that you do not have to
> > deal to win an English tourney. It may help, and some of the best
> > players may well be defined by their abilities to deal (no hard
> > feelings Rob:-), but games are generally played at the level of the
> > decks on the table not of the people playing those decks.
>
> >But it is not the only way and it is certainly
> > not the best way.
> >
> > Tony
>
> Have to disagree with you there on a massive scale Tony (did you expect any
> less ?). I am totally of the belief that a consistently successful player
> uses all means to win at his / her disposal. This includes (where
> appropriate to deck type and situation) the full range of agitation and deal
> making skills.
>

The point I was trying to make, was that a deck has a set deal and
agitation potential attached to it. It will obviously vary, but Some
decks lend themselves to agitation to the level of not being able to
perform without it. Whereas others have little or no amunition to deal
(mine for example). Once the deck is made and playtested the deck
becomes the template for the deals made, not the player (again I'm
talking in degrees, not absolutes), the tables, players and luck of
draw all plays a part but only in relation to how they enter the orbit
of your deck. the deck is your army, the table the land you wish to
conquer. and agitation is an extra regiment that some decks make use
of. but, because all the men in that regiment are drunks, it can be
difficult to control, so only a skilled general can marshall them.

(sorry about that shameless extended metaphor, it was the only way I
could think of to make any sense whatsoever)

> As I have said in many of my newsletters and general commentary, the player
> who actively decides 'not to deal' is IMO robbing themselves of one of the
> sharpest swords in the game.

But a player resolutely refusing to deal can have a crippling effect
on a deck with agitation as a key strategy. In fact, I'd be interested
to see you experiment with a deck designed to remain in a bubble of
forward motion and fuck decks that need table balance. 20 kindred
spirits maybe?

>
> I put it to you that you won by taking advantage of a good opportunity,
> having little or no pressure on you, playing your focussed deck well and NOT
> AT ALL by declining to make deals. As we discussed at length at the tourney,
> your deck did not lend itself at all to deal making (I guess
> counterproductive cross table Deflections would be about all it could offer)
> and as such no player on the table sought to make deals with you. All being
> experienced 'identification players' we had seen what your deck did and knew
> exactly what you intended to do with it :o) Which is exactly why you felt
> 'left out' of the deal making on the table.

I didn't say that I won because I didn't make deals. I said I won
without making deals.

I didn't voice my objection to well at the tourney, due to alcohol and
having some rapidly overproductive sweat glands. But my problem was
not that I felt "left out" (god that makes me sound like I was the
last picked for football at playtime). I have played enough decks to
know that if you have no dick it's pointless trying to shag (so to
speak). My problem was that I felt I had wandered into a game where
everyone was wary and scared of everyone else except me. I won yes,
but I still felt out of my league and I hate that feeling. I have only
been playing the game for about 7 months, so I don't expect to be a
big and feared juggernaut of terror (like your good self), but it
would have been nice to get a little recognition. When you burnt
Arika, you didn't consider me getting that vp a problem. Fair enough,
the deck had to go, or he would have won, so no arguements here. After
matt went, you offered a 1st and 2nd deal to Will, who was getting
pounded by me. Admittedly I probably wouldn't have taken the deal as i
was confident I could kill you both. You discarded a rush when i had 5
minions out, Now this I wasn't too sure about. You must have known
that Will had more than enough ammo to burn a few of my minions, one
more from you may have made a big difference. You parity shifted Will
making it easier for me to kill him. Now all this was a tad baffling
to me. Again, I would never claim to be as skilled at the game as any
of the other people at that table, but these moves (with the exception
of burning Arika) all seem to point to me not really being a threat
until it was too late. That was my problem, no the deal thing. Maybe
I'm being a little petulant but it did annoy me at the time.

>
> The sort of deck that you played tends to be seen by others as a huge threat
> to the balance of the table. In any other situation I would have had no
> qualms what so ever in enlisting the help of any / all other players on the
> table to stamp on a Weenie deck. Part of my (and many, many other players)
> game centres around balancing the table and talking to achieve such an end.
> A deck such as yours is bound to unsettle as it can oust very quickly and
> comes out of the blocks bleeding for 6-10 per turn.
>
> In hindsight, had I known that you were packing 10 Deflections (you filthy
> man :o) there is no way I would have chosen to bleed you, but then again
> Francois would have very possibly sat down somewhere different after me.
> Ideally I should have sat behind Francios with you bleeding me, but as I
> said - hindsight... bloody table order :o(

I only had 6 or 7, I forget. I was bleeding will knowing full well I
couldn't get through just to cycle cards. I did pitch a few masters to
stop Chaz just to cycle cards, so I was churning through my deck
looking for them. If it looked like it was that sleezy, I apologize.
But I did have to work hard to stay alive at the end, knowing that if
I blocked I'd most likely get torpored and not have enough minions to
bleed out Will.

>
> I would also add as an aside that had you chosen to make deals, it would IMO
> have only served to strengthen your table position and make your job easier.
> Even a player playing a weenie dom or pre deck can establish others as the
> bad guys on the table and enlist aid in taking them down.

I was a bit too nervous to try and deal.

>
> Again, extremely well done for winning man, but don't lose sight of the
> final that we played.

I was analysing it long after we stopped. But thanks man.
>
Tony
